(i) we propose an algorithmic framework for federated learning that combines global and local methods and (ii) we instantiate algorithms that are near-optimal for strongly convex problems and achieve improved rates for convex and nonconvex problems.
we propose FedChain, a novel framework that combines the benefits of global and local methods in federated learning.

(i) FedChain is a framework for combining the benefits of local and global methods, (ii) we provide a novel lower bound on the number of rounds needed to achieve a target accuracy, (iii) we provide new algorithms for FedAvg and PL problems, (iv) we show that FedChain achieves a near-optimal rate in the strong convexity setting.

the following question: Can we design a federated learning algorithm with near-optimal communication complexity and fast convergence in terms the number of communication round?

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our work proposes a novel approach to federated learning that achieves fast convergence in terms communication rounds and leverages the similarity between clients' local data.
FedChain achieves the fastest known convergence rate in terms of R in the convex setting and is near-optimal in the strongly convex setting.
we propose a new algorithmic framework that is near-optimal in the general convex setting, and improves upon existing methods in the PL and strong convexity settings.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
FedChain achieves the best of both worlds: it is fast in terms of communication complexity while also leveraging the similarity between data across clients.
FedChain can achieve near-optimal communication complexity while retaining fast convergence in terms R.
FedChain is a general and powerful framework for designing communication-efficient algorithms for FL.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, by carefully combining local updates with global updates in a principled way, one can achieve the best of both worlds in federated learning.
the communication complexity of federated learning is fundamentally different than that of centralized machine learning, and that this can be exploited to design more efficient algorithms.
the communication complexity of distributed training in FL is fundamentally different from that of distributed training in the centralized setting.
